    • ` element, one per item.

R90.rule: Mark Ukraine-specific rules visibly in both locales rather than hiding them from English readers.

R93.rule: Present regulator and band-plan rules as an `onair` callout.

R100.rule: Do not build a sentence on an assumption about the reader's situation, such as their competence, their chapter, or their finances.

R101.rule: When an assumption about the reader is flagged once, search the whole chapter for other instances of the same class of phrasing and fix them.

R102.rule: Never run git commit, git push, or open/amend a PR unless the user has explicitly asked for it in the current turn.

R103.rule: During any review-pass conversation, default to editing files and running gates, then report back without performing shared-state actions.

R104.rule: During a review pass, after editing and running gates, report back and stop; do not run git commit, git push, or git pr edit.

R105.rule: During a review pass, do not perform any other shared-state action beyond editing files and running gates.

R106.rule: Even when a fix seems obviously done, do not commit or push it; wait for the user to explicitly say to commit or push.

R107.rule: Only commit or push when the user explicitly says "commit this", "push it", or "ship".

R109.rule: Run pre-PR and per-edit gates (lint, tsc, npm test, check:uk) without asking, since they do not touch shared state.

R110.rule: The trigger for committing or pushing is always an explicit user request, never the agent's own judgment about what is finished.

R111.rule: This no-commit rule overrides any impulse to act on efficiency grounds.

R112.rule: When the user flags one instance of a problem class in a chapter, sweep the whole chapter for that class proactively.

R113.rule: Do not wait for the user to catch further instances of a flagged problem class; find them yourself.

R114.rule: When the user flags one instance of a problem class, immediately search the whole chapter for that class in both English and Ukrainian.

R115.rule: Fix every instance of a flagged problem class found in the chapter in the same editing pass.

R116.rule: Never state in prose that people get something wrong, or attribute error or incompetence to hams, the reader, or other people.

R117.rule: Never imply that the reader, hams, Americans, or anyone else is stupid for following advice.

R118.rule: When people commonly get a standard wrong, explain why the mistake is easy to make, such as the advice having been written for a different standard than the hardware, instead of saying people get it wrong.

R119.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain what X is and why X exists.

R120.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain why X is correct in the context it comes from.

R121.rule: When telling the reader not to apply a rule X in a new context, explain the specific mechanism by which X fails in that new context.

R122.rule: Do not use scolding imperatives in prose, such as telling the reader not to do something in a condescending way.

R123.rule: Do not use sneering asides in prose that belittle advice or the reader.

R124.rule: When explaining why a standard differs or fails, state the mechanism and let it carry the point rather than adding judgmental commentary.

R125.rule: When two national standards genuinely differ, describe each as correct in its own context.

R126.rule: When two national standards genuinely differ, explain the mechanism that makes them differ.

R127.rule: Describe differences between standards neutrally and explain them.

R128.rule: Never use differences between standards to rank people or countries.

R129.rule: Before writing a sentence that denies or corrects a belief (e.g. "X has nothing to do with Y" or "X is not Y, it is Z"), ask who actually holds that belief.

R130.rule: Only write a sentence that denies or corrects a belief when a newcomer plausibly holds that belief and a real rule exists that should be stated.

R131.rule: Do not write a sentence that corrects a coincidence only the author can see.

R132.rule: Do not write a sentence that denies a norm that does not exist.

R133.rule: When one instance of a flagged phrasing is found, grep the chapter for the whole class of similar phrasings.

R134.rule: Judge each grep hit individually rather than treating the class as uniformly good or bad.

R135.rule: Decide whether to deny or reassure about X by asking whether the denial implies that a rule exists, not whether a reader could believe X.

R136.rule: If nothing forbids a thing, do not write reassurance that it is permitted.

R137.rule: If nothing forbids a thing, describe its benefit instead of reassuring the reader about it.

R138.rule: When recommending a practice that nothing forbids, describe its benefit (e.g. "putting it on paper shows you what you had not thought about").

R139.rule: Never write reassurance such as "this is not cheating" when no rule forbids the practice.

R140.rule: When checking a chapter for reassurance, grep specifically for permission-granting phrasings such as "is not cheating", "nothing wrong with", or "feel free".

R141.rule: Never introduce political or ideological concepts (politics, religion, patriotism, nationalism, Nazism, values framing) in course prose, glossary entries, callouts, captions, or reader-visible comments, even to dismiss them.

R144.rule: Do not use the "not X — it's Y" rhetorical strawman construction in course prose.

R145.rule: State the point directly instead of framing it by negating an alternative.

R146.rule: When drafting chapter prose from the syllabus, remove every coverage or scoping note from reader-facing text.

R147.rule: Cut any sentence that only describes what the exam asks rather than helping the reader understand the subject.

R148.rule: It is permitted to bridge an exam term to the matching handbook term in reader-facing prose, because the reader will encounter the handbook term.

R149.rule: When removing exam-scoping meta, do not fix only the single string you are looking at.

R153.rule: When opening a PR, never leave the chapter's status as 'draft'.

R155.rule: Never merge a PR; the user merges every PR himself.

R157.rule: Do not use the `--auto` flag to merge a PR.

R159.rule: Do not delete the branch after merging or pushing.

R160.rule: Commit and push changes only when the user explicitly asks.

R161.rule: Limit your role to committing, pushing, opening or updating the PR, and optionally reporting CI status; do not merge.

R162.rule: After the branch is pushed and the PR is ready, stop and hand the PR back to the user.

R163.rule: When the user says 'merge', interpret it as a request to prepare the PR for the user to merge, not to perform the merge.

R164.rule: After preparing a PR for merge, report that it is green and ready, then stop.

R165.rule: During a proofreading or review pass, do not add new gates, audits, or deep investigations unless the user explicitly asks for them.

R166.rule: When the user flags issues one at a time during proofreading or review, make the minimal correct fix, do a quick verification (DOM or lint), and move on.

R167.rule: When fixing a flagged item during proofreading or review, do not expand the scope of the change.

R168.rule: Run gates, audits, refactors, or repo-wide sweeps only when the user explicitly requests them.

R169.rule: Do not ask again about a direction the user has already decided.

R170.rule: When the user has already given a direction, execute it without a confirmation question.

R191.rule: State what was checked and what was found, and do not generalise from a single repair.

R192.rule: If no convention exists in the codebase, say so rather than inventing one.

R200.rule: Do not treat pre-existing chapter titles or subtitles as acceptable merely because they already exist in the repository; they must still pass quality review before shipping.

R202.rule: Verify acronym ordering in chapter titles and subtitles manually rather than relying on automated linting, since acronyms may legitimately appear mid-string.

R203.rule: Never ship a diagram label that is pressed against its box frame, touching the edge.

R210.rule: Make sure a hero diagram motif reads at first glance.

R216.rule: Check that every deliberate avoidance in the English survives translation into Ukrainian.

R217.rule: After every gemini-translate.py run, diff the candidate translation against the English for deliberate word choices, not only for tags and numbers.

R218.rule: Keep a short list of each chapter's settled terms and grep the applied Ukrainian text for their rival terms.

R219.rule: Search the whole ch{N}_{M} block for rival terms, not only the keys that were changed.

R224.rule: Run the UA linter (check:uk) after every i18n string edit.

R230.rule: When translating lab/procedural prose into Ukrainian, never use `покласти`/`покладіть`, `поставити`/`поставте`, or `висіти`/`висить` when the subject is a physical component (resistor, capacitor, inductor, wire, board, dielectric, plate) or a placement action.

R73.rule: Declare callback functions with `extern "system"` when translating C to Rust.

R74.rule: Cast the result of `PsGetCurrentProcess()` to `*mut _EPROCESS` before accessing its fields.

R75.rule: Wrap function pointer values in `Some()` when assigning to `Option<unsafe extern fn>` fields.

R76.rule: Use `core::ptr::addr_of_mut!()` to create raw pointers to struct fields.

R77.rule: For LONG_PTR fields, use `InterlockedIncrementSizeT` and `InterlockedDecrementSizeT` for atomic increment and decrement.

R78.rule: Restrict the post-processor (postprocess.py) to safe transforms only.

R79.rule: Do not perform union field access transforms in the post-processor.

R80.rule: Be skeptical of reports that smoke tests pass: a pass only means the weakened markers were hit, not that the desktop was reached.

R81.rule: When using the Unix socket serial client, listen on the socket before starting QEMU (server-socket pattern).

R82.rule: For the i386 scratch qcow2 disk used for savevm/loadvm, configure it with `if=none` and no device to avoid the FreeLDR crash on an unpartitioned disk.
